name: Leersia

project_scope.selection_mode: FINISH/ENRICH existing canonical Leersia species only
project_scope.native_zone_review: Preserve species PROVISIONAL and native_metrics_excluded fields; no BONAP/NAPA county recertification.

look_here_first: ONE INSTALLED SPECIES: Leersia oryzoides (rice cutgrass). Check for backward-pointing sharp microscopic leaf-margin SPINULES (with lens, not fingers), then find an OPEN wavy panicle with flat rice-grain-like AWNLESS spikelets. In full flowering head L. oryzoides usually has two or more PRIMARY branches at lowest panicle nodes; white cutgrass (L. virginica) commonly has one. Mature rice-cutgrass spikelets are ~4.2–6.5 mm, versus white cutgrass often ~2.2–4 mm; ranges can overlap and records can be confused. True membranous ligule ~0.5–1 mm. Neither photo shows the diagnostic backwards teeth or lowest node correctly enough to arrow.

recognition.where_to_look_first: A wet-edge perennial rhizomatous grass with broad rather harsh blades, panicles of narrow tiny rice-like flat spikelets, and the very short collar membrane. First photograph a margin tooth at macro scale. Then measure a single flattened spikelet, count low panicle branch number, and examine an underground rhizome only if allowed.
priority: wet creek/ditch/marsh vegetation; perennial creeping stems
blade margins strongly retrose-scabrous; avoid skin cuts
leaf sheaths often quite rough; stem nodes may have short white hair bands
slender open panicle, often 2 or more low branches per node
narrow flattened single-flowered spikelets approx 4–6.5 mm, essentially without glumes
long creeping rhizomes with loosely spaced/non-overlapping scales
recognition.field_safe_handling: Never swipe a bare finger along the sharp blade edge; use a hand lens and hold gently near the blade base.

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: CUTTING TEETH (NEED A REAL MACRO) + 2+ LOWEST PANICLE BRANCHES (NEED WHOLE NODE) + 4.2–6.5 MM FLAT RICE SPIKELETS (NEED RULER) = RICE CUTGRASS CANDIDATE, not an unqualified ID.
quick_split: L. oryzoides (rice cutgrass) — exceptionally rough backward-prickled margins; usually 2+ branches at the LOWEST panicle node; narrow spikelets ~4.2–6.5 mm; elongated rhizomes with nonoverlapping scales.
L. virginica (white cutgrass) — typically smoother sheaths, often ONE basal panicle branch; smaller ~2.2–4 mm spikelets that may crowd each other; short rhizomes with closely overlapping scales.
L. lenticularis — broad disk/coin-shaped spikelets, not narrow rice grains; examine a mature spikelet face and side.
Zizaniopsis miliacea — giant cutgrass, conspicuously larger robust marsh-grass stature and different panicle/spikelet organization; cutting margin alone not enough.
Zizania texana — protected endangered Texas wild-rice; don't uproot or handle for a comparison, identify non-invasively using whole aquatic flowering structures.
Paspalum spp. — flowering axis spikelets in other arrangements; photograph fertile florets and branch points, not just a grass growing by water.
comparison_lesson.verification_rule: One source-labelled photo of narrow spikelets does not independently establish the specimen's retrorse leaf margin, lowermost panicle branch number, missing glumes or attached rootstock. For species-level comparison with L. virginica, record 2+ same-node branches and a mature mm-scaled spikelet, plus membrane ligule, from a SINGLE attached same plant.

lookalikes.field_split: Usually more delicate with smoother or only moderately rough leaf sheaths. Flowering head generally has ONE branch at a low node rather than two or more; small spikelets (~2.4–4 mm) often crowded/overlapping more strongly; short closely overlapping rhizome scales. Mature paired-branch and spikelet counts are more reliable than wet habitat alone.
lookalikes.photo_need: Whole panicle lower branching node and single spikelet with mm reference; correct source-labelled specimen.

lookalikes.field_split: Spikelets are broad and round or lens-shaped rather than elongate narrow 'rice grains'; may be nearly circular and often look like little disks. Large leaf blades may be similarly rough, so seek mature spikelet dimensions and outline.
lookalikes.photo_need: Spikelets from face and edge, with mm ruler and attached pedicel.

lookalikes.field_split: Much taller robust marsh grass with broad blades and a large branching panicle whose reproductive spikelets are organized differently; compare whole plant scale and flowering structures, not sharp leaf edges alone.
lookalikes.photo_need: Whole stand and size comparison plus panicle close-up.

lookalikes.field_split: Aquatic perennial from flowing river channels with dramatically different pollen- and seed-bearing branches. Do not mistake any narrow water-edge grass leaf for this endangered localized aquatic grass. Species diagnosis and stewardship need the actual inflorescence and habitat context.
lookalikes.photo_need: Legal non-disturbing habitat and clear flowering anatomy; never uproot protected wild-rice.

lookalikes.field_split: Many one-sided racemes bear two-flowered spikelets and a membranous ligule. Leersia typically has very rough leaf surfaces/margins, more flexible open panicle branches, and flattened one-flowered spikelets with no evident glumes.
lookalikes.photo_need: Matched leaf-edge and flowering branch + single spikelet macro.

comparison_matrix.title: Rice cutgrass versus two other cutgrasses
rows: Sharply retrorse rough margins and sheath
Usually smoother sheaths, less harsh margins
Blade margin + lower branch node + mm spikelet

what_to_teach_crew: Cutgrass may scratch: inspect a leaf edge with a hand lens, DO NOT slide a bare finger or hand along a leaf blade.
Find and photograph the entire same-plant flowering panicle; count branches at its FIRST/LOWEST branching node (often 2+ in rice cutgrass).
Photograph a single mature, narrow rice-shaped flattened spikelet with a 1-mm ruler: ~4.2–6.5 mm for rice cutgrass; glumes not conspicuous.
Compare WHITE CUTGRASS L. virginica: generally one branch at lowest panicle node and smaller less widely spaced spikelets; do not rely on surface roughness alone.
Compare broadly coin-shaped L. lenticularis, giant-cutgrass Zizaniopsis, and endangered Texas wild-rice non-invasively; wet habitat does not equal the same taxon.
Use the existing photos for WHAT AN OPEN PANICLE LOOKS LIKE; remember both pictures lack the actual cutting-edge-teeth detail.
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 1 installed taxon; two CC BY source-labelled JPEGs with four true gross arrows. Critical leaf-margin teeth, lowermost panicle branch node, actual glume-reduced measured spikelet, attached ligule and rhizomes not imaged.
visual_needs: PRIORITY diagnostic gap: a true source-verified rice-cutgrass leaf edge with BACKWARD-directed minute stiff TEETH at 10–20× and metric scale; external Go Botany image is useful for study only, licensing not cleared for website.
Second: whole mature panicle LOWEST rachis node with 2+ attached branches in same photo, side-by-side with L. virginica one-lowest-branch comparison (not demonstrated in existing images).
Third: 1-flowered narrow flat rice-like spikelet measured ~4.2–6.5 mm, glume-reduced/absent base and keel fringe separately resolvable.
Fourth: actual short membranous ligule 0.5–1 mm and blade/sheath junction from the same specimen.
Fifth: same plant rooted riparian habitat photo with running rhizome and known attachment of leaf and flowering stems; wetland disruption minimized.

Current public visual lesson: two physically stored Sam Kieschnick CC BY reproductive photos, four visible arrows, no unseen tooth/collar/rhizome claims; stored Joey study frame excluded until verified separately.

visual_comparison.title: Leersia — photographed narrow rice spikelets, elusive cutting teeth
visual_comparison.subtitle: One current species: rice cutgrass. Two physically archived CC BY Sam Kieschnick photo panels, FOUR defensible gross-structure arrows. Do not label unseen serrated leaf edges, a proven branch pair at the lowest node, membrane ligule or glumeless spikelet base.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Wetland grass → very ROUGH/RETRORSE leaf edge → 2+ branches often at LOWEST panicle nodes → narrow 4.2–6.5 mm one-flowered rice-like spikelets. Need actual photo and lens proof; don't scrape fingers on leaves.

items.image_role: Source-labelled Leersia oryzoides spikelets arranged on delicate branching panicle; photographed against a hand for scale

Separate spikelets and a thin panicle branch are resolved; the hand is only approximate scale. The photograph does NOT separately resolve glumes, keel cilia, pedicel base, or a millimeter measurement.
items.why_it_matters: Recognize the distinct flattened rice-grain-like spikelets on fine branching stalks; inspect a whole mature spikelet and panicle node for exact species ID.
